summary: This informational memo gives a taxonomy of architectures in existing IEEE 802.11 products. It analyses wireless LAN functions and describes how they are split between entities such as access points and controllers.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4118 organizes wireless LAN designs by where they perform Wi-Fi and network-management functions. It describes three main families and three ways to divide work in centralized designs.

subtitle: A taxonomy of how wireless LAN functions are divided among access points and controllers.

tldr.problem: IEEE 802.11 leaves many implementation details open, so vendors placed WLAN functions across devices in different ways with mostly proprietary interfaces.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines terms and classifies surveyed architectures as Autonomous, Centralized, or Distributed Mesh; Centralized designs include Local MAC, Split MAC, and Remote MAC variants.
tldr.outcome: The taxonomy provides common terms for comparing existing designs and discusses the interfaces needed when functions are split across network devices.

today: RFC 4118 is an Informational taxonomy published in June 2005. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Classify WLAN Architectures
sections.content:
Managing many IEEE 802.11 access points can burden network administrators. Large WLANs also need consistent configuration and coordination of the shared radio medium.

Vendors developed different solutions, often with proprietary interfaces. This memo provides a taxonomy of architectures in existing WLAN products to give standards groups and others a common view of those designs.
sections.plainLanguage: Large Wi-Fi networks need many access points to work together, but vendors divide the work differently. This memo organizes those designs into common categories.

sections.title: 802.11 Functions and CAPWAP Functions
sections.content:
IEEE 802.11 defines functions for wireless stations and distribution systems, including authentication, association, frame delivery, beacons, retransmissions, and rate adaptation. The standard does not require all these functions to run in one physical device.

The memo calls management and control functions not directly defined by 802.11 CAPWAP functions. Examples include radio monitoring, channel configuration, firmware loading, station-state information, and authentication between a Wireless Termination Point (WTP) and an Access Controller (AC). A logical access point may span physical devices.
sections.plainLanguage: 802.11 functions handle wireless communication. CAPWAP functions help configure and manage a WLAN, and a physical WTP can provide only part of the logical access point's functions.

sections.title: Three WLAN Architecture Families
sections.content:
In an Autonomous WLAN, each WTP implements the 802.11 and relevant CAPWAP functions. In a Centralized WLAN, functions are divided between WTPs and one or more ACs. In a Distributed Mesh WLAN, peer nodes relay traffic and can share control functions.

The memo further divides Centralized WLANs by where the 802.11 MAC functions run. Local MAC keeps most or all MAC functions at the WTP; Split MAC divides them between WTP and AC; Remote MAC places the MAC at the AC while the WTP handles the radio PHY.
sections.plainLanguage: Autonomous designs keep the work at each WTP, centralized designs divide it between WTPs and ACs, and mesh designs use peer nodes. Centralized designs differ in where they place the 802.11 MAC functions.

sections.title: Centralized Design Choices
sections.content:
WTPs and ACs may connect directly, through Layer 2 switches, or through Layer 3 routers. Local MAC and Split MAC designs can support routed connections in many surveyed implementations. Remote MAC has tighter timing requirements because the AC performs the MAC functions.

Local MAC keeps more station state at the WTP. Remote MAC centralizes more state and leaves the WTP simpler. Split MAC places time-sensitive functions such as beacon generation at the WTP and many other functions at the AC, though vendors do not split every function the same way.
sections.plainLanguage: Centralized designs balance local processing against central control. Remote MAC needs tighter timing between WTP and AC; Local MAC keeps more work at each WTP.

sections.title: Security and Interoperability
sections.content:
Centralized designs add a control relationship between WTP and AC. The memo discusses secure discovery, authentication, and confidentiality, integrity, and replay protection for control-channel traffic. Centralizing secrets can reduce the risk from a stolen WTP, but makes the AC a valuable target.

Mesh nodes need to authenticate one another within the same administrative domain. The memo recommends protecting communication between neighboring nodes. It also says that proprietary interfaces among vendors' architectures limit interoperability and that interfaces are needed when functions are split across devices.
sections.plainLanguage: WTPs and ACs need secure discovery and protected control traffic, while mesh nodes need to authenticate each other. Common interfaces are needed for devices from different vendors to work together.
